title: Choose the visual world — Shadoword website
question: The roll assigned Bench Instrument. Keep it, take an alternate, or re-roll.

options.label: Bench Instrument
options.lineage: Braun ET / audio-300 era functional instrument panels
options.thesis: Shadoword is not an app with a landing page; it is an instrument on your desk, so the page is its front panel — and it refuses the near-black dev-tool site with one neon accent.
options.viewport: Full viewport is one instrument face at physical scale, cropped by the frame: a large black perforated grille field on the left, and on the right a control column carrying a three-position OFF / LOCAL / REMOTE selector detented on LOCAL and lit orange, a tick-scale latency readout with an indexed needle, and the primary action as a chamfered push-button to the source repo. One line of real display type sits on the top legend plate; every other word on screen is 11-13px screen-printed legend type. That inversion — huge panel, tiny legends, one big line — is the whole design.
options.risk: Instrument-scale type is small by nature. If the single large hook line is not set decisively, or if the perforated grille is faked with a lazy CSS dot pattern instead of an authored pitch-correct texture, the page reads as cheap minimalism instead of a made object.

options.label: Safelight Bay
options.thesis: A light-tight room where the work never leaves until you carry it out — the offline claim as a place, with transcription staged as an image emerging in the tray.
options.case: Strongest fusion of the hand: the station sequence (compose, expose, develop, fix) maps exactly onto capture, segment, commit, deliver, and a darkroom IS an airgap. Wins audience identification, loses product clarity: the darkroom's entire emotional grammar is patience and irreversibility, and Shadoword sells low latency and cheap retries. The world would be arguing against the product.

options.label: Phosphor Grid
options.lineage: pixel-art arcade cabinet screen, scanlines and phosphor bloom
options.thesis: Sixteen colors on phosphor black, whole-tile composition, and the black between scanlines doing half the work; voice level and transcript both live on one integer-scaled grid.
options.case: Retrocomputing is native culture for a Linux developer, so identification is high, and phosphor glow is genuinely adjacent to a waveform display. Loses product clarity twice over: an arcade cabinet frames the product as a toy when the ask is a private dictation tool a skeptic will trust, and bloom plus reserved flashing white-gold fights the calm, precise voice PRODUCT.md commits to.

options.label: Sliding Planes
options.thesis: One continuous space partitioned by sliding planes, primary color rationed to only the edges that actually move — local and remote are plane positions, not pages.
options.case: The reconfiguration idea fuses well with the product's real duality (one core, two shapes) and View Transitions would make layout itself the navigation. But identification is weak: De Stijl is design-canon literacy, not this audience's daily world, and red-yellow-blue planes read playful where the page has to read trustworthy about audio privacy.

canonCard.label: The category standard
canonCard.thesis: The dev-tool landing page every open-source project ships, executed impeccably rather than ironically.
canonCard.viewport: Near-black ground, one accent, a centered headline over a subhead and two buttons, a terminal install snippet in a rounded card, then a six-item feature grid, a comparison table, and an FAQ. Exactly what your current site is, done properly.
canonCard.risk: Indistinguishable from the ten other transcription projects a visitor saw this month; nothing about it is memorable an hour later.
